Pregnancy

Dry eyes in pregnancy: symptoms, safe care and when to seek help

Updated: November 4, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Pregnancy can change how the surface of the eye feels, and some people develop gritty, burning or unusually watery eyes. Hormonal changes may contribute, but they do not explain every new eye symptom. An eye examination can distinguish dry eye from other problems and help you choose treatment that fits pregnancy or breastfeeding.

Recognising discomfort without overlooking a warning sign

Dry eye may cause stinging, burning, itching, a gritty sensation, tired eyes, mild redness or extra watering. The tear film can be unstable even when tears run down your cheeks. Contact lenses and prolonged reading or screen work may become uncomfortable; symptoms alone cannot establish the diagnosis.

Blurred vision, light sensitivity, substantial pain, pus-like discharge or difficulty seeing at night should not simply be filed under normal pregnancy dryness. Sticky lids may also reflect an eyelid problem or infection. Report new visual symptoms promptly, and use the urgent eye and maternity advice below rather than waiting to see whether a lubricant fixes them.

How pregnancy may affect the tear film

Tears contain water, mucus and oils that help cover and protect the eye when you blink. Dry eye can occur when there are too few tears, they evaporate too quickly or their composition and spreading are disturbed. The eyelids and their oil glands matter as well as the glands that produce watery tears.

Pregnancy-related hormonal and fluid changes may affect tear function, the cornea and contact-lens comfort. These associations do not prove that hormones caused an individual episode, or that one trimester is the inevitable worst stage. A change in pressure inside the eye is not a reason to assume that dryness is protective or harmless.

Other contributors still need consideration

Direct heating or air-conditioning airflow, wind, smoke, dry indoor air and long periods of screen use can aggravate symptoms. Contact lenses may add irritation. Some medicines, eyelid inflammation, allergy and other health conditions can contribute, and more than one factor can be present.

Tell the eye-care professional about current medicines, drops, supplements, allergies and any previous eye disease. Mention diabetes, high blood pressure, kidney disease and your pregnancy stage to the maternity team as appropriate. Do not stop a prescribed medicine because you suspect it causes dryness; ask the prescriber to review the options.

What an assessment can clarify

An optometrist or ophthalmologist can assess your vision, the eye surface, eyelids and tear film. They may use a lighted examination and tests of tear production or how quickly tears break up, depending on the findings. Not everyone needs the same tests, and a photograph or online symptom checklist cannot replace the examination.

Arrange assessment if discomfort persists, recurs or interferes with daily life, or if you keep needing drops without relief. An eye assessment and maternity assessment answer different questions: checking the surface of the eye does not replace pregnancy blood-pressure or urine checks. Warning symptoms need urgent care rather than a routine appointment.

Everyday changes that may improve comfort

Take regular breaks from close work and make an effort to blink fully. Position the screen comfortably, reduce direct fan or air-conditioning flow towards your face and avoid smoke. Glasses or wraparound sunglasses can help shield the eyes from wind outdoors; choose proper sun protection rather than assuming any dark lens is protective.

A humidifier may help in a dry room if cleaned and used according to its instructions. Keep comfort measures practical: adding houseplants is not a treatment for dry-eye disease, and changing the room cannot treat an infection or pregnancy complication. Use glasses when lenses are uncomfortable and seek advice when symptoms do not settle.

Food, fluids and supplements

Eat a varied diet and drink regularly according to your needs and any advice from your maternity team. Dehydration or a genuine nutritional deficiency needs appropriate assessment; drinking excessive water or adding vitamins is not a guaranteed dry-eye treatment. Continue recommended pregnancy supplements for their intended purpose, not as a promised cure for eye symptoms.

Do not self-treat dryness with high-dose supplements, vitamin A/retinol or cod-liver oil in pregnancy; avoid liver and check supplement labels with your clinician or pharmacist. A large trial in adults with dry eye found that omega-3 supplements did not improve outcomes more than placebo. It was not a pregnancy treatment trial, and does not establish a pregnancy dose, benefit or safety plan.

Gentle eyelid care and remedies to avoid

If an eye-care professional recommends eyelid hygiene, a clean cloth moistened with comfortably warm water can be held against closed lids, followed by gentle cleaning or lid care as instructed. Avoid hot compresses, forceful rubbing or pressure on the eyeball. Stop if the method hurts or irritates the skin, and do not substitute it for assessment of a painful red eye.

Do not put homemade rose water, herbal mixtures, oils or water into the eyes as treatment. Boiling and cooling water does not make a home preparation a validated sterile eye-drop product. A cloth used externally on closed lids is different from instilling liquid into the eye. Products intended for the skin or face are not automatically suitable for eyes.

Choosing lubricants during pregnancy

Artificial tears are lubricating drops, but formulations differ. A pharmacist or eye-care professional can check the exact ingredients and product, your lens use and how often you need it. NHS guidance specifically permits carmellose sodium eye drops during pregnancy and breastfeeding; this does not mean that every product marketed for red or irritated eyes has the same evidence.

Ask for advice before using antibiotic, steroid, allergy or redness-relief drops, or changing a prescribed eye treatment. Some medicated drops may be needed after an individual benefit–risk assessment; pregnancy is not a reason to stop them all. Preservative-free options may be considered if drops are frequent or irritating, but the whole formulation and correct use still matter.

Using and storing drops carefully

Wash your hands and follow the exact product instructions. Do not let the bottle tip touch your eye, lashes, fingers or another surface, and do not share drops. Check expiry and the time allowed after opening; follow the leaflet for single-use containers rather than assuming they can all be reused.

For carmellose, NHS instructions advise gently closing the eye and pressing the inner corner for about a minute after a drop. If several eye medicines are prescribed, follow the professional's order and spacing instructions. Remove contact lenses when the product requires it and respect its reinsertion interval. Stop the product and seek advice if it causes pain, discharge or a vision change; urgent warning signs need urgent care.

Contact lenses may need a break

Pregnancy does not automatically ban contact lenses, but dryness or changes in the cornea can make them less comfortable. Remove lenses when they irritate your eyes and use glasses while you get advice. More cleaning or wearing the lenses for fewer hours does not make it safe to ignore a red or painful eye.

Wash and dry your hands before handling lenses, use the recommended disinfecting solution and avoid water exposure, including showering or swimming in lenses. Do not top up old solution with fresh solution or sleep in lenses unless specifically instructed by your eye-care professional. A red eye in a contact-lens wearer needs urgent assessment even if pain is mild or absent.

After birth: improvement is possible, but the timing varies

Pregnancy-related eye changes often improve after delivery, and some may take longer, including during breastfeeding. There is no reliable promise that every dry-eye symptom will disappear within a few weeks. Persistent symptoms may have another contributor and should be reassessed instead of waiting indefinitely for hormones to settle.

Tell your clinician if you are breastfeeding when reviewing treatments. Continue any agreed eye-care plan and ask about persistent discomfort or a changed glasses or lens prescription. New visual symptoms after birth still need prompt assessment: pre-eclampsia can first appear after delivery, so it should not be dismissed because the pregnancy has ended.

When to seek urgent eye or maternity care

Contact your maternity team immediately for new blurred vision, flashing lights, spots, altered colour vision or another visual change during pregnancy or after birth. A severe headache, pain below the ribs, sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet, heartburn that does not improve with heartburn medicine, vomiting or feeling very unwell also needs immediate maternity advice; you do not need all these symptoms or a known high blood pressure. Pre-eclampsia and other conditions require assessment, not a diagnosis from an eye symptom alone.

Seek urgent assessment for a painful red eye or a red eye while wearing contact lenses. Get emergency care for a new change or loss of sight, pain when looking at light, a red eye with a severe headache and nausea, a very dark-red eye, an injured or punctured eye, or something stuck in the eye; you do not need all these signs, and do not drive yourself. Tell the service that you are pregnant or recently gave birth so eye and maternity care can be coordinated. Do not delay because symptoms might be dryness or while waiting for an ordinary eye appointment.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ophthalmology and optometry guidance recognises pregnancy-related tear and corneal changes, but individual symptoms need assessment and postpartum recovery is variable.

NEI, NHS, CDC and FDA guidance supports cause-directed eye care, suitable lubricants, contact-lens and drop hygiene, and avoiding unvalidated eye preparations. Carmellose has specific pregnancy and breastfeeding guidance.

NHS eye and pre-eclampsia guidance requires prompt action for visual changes and other warning symptoms. Nutrition advice and adult omega-3 evidence do not justify high-dose supplementation as a pregnancy dry-eye cure.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you record symptoms, lens use, drop names and questions for your eye-care and maternity teams. It cannot diagnose dry eye, assess eye pressure, rule out pre-eclampsia or decide that a medicine is suitable for you.

When to seek help

Do not put homemade remedies into the eyes or stop prescribed drops without advice. New visual symptoms during pregnancy or after birth need immediate assessment. A painful red eye or a red eye with contact lenses needs urgent eye care. New sight change or loss, pain looking at light, or a red eye with severe headache and nausea needs emergency care; do not drive yourself or wait for all symptoms.

Evidence notes updated: November 4, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Pregnancy may affect tear function, but not every gritty, watery or uncomfortable eye is caused by hormones.
  • Persistent symptoms deserve an eye examination; pregnancy blood-pressure checks remain important.
  • Screen breaks, less direct airflow, a lens break and suitable lubricants may help. Avoid homemade eye preparations.
  • Check the exact drop product in pregnancy or breastfeeding; do not stop prescribed treatment without advice.
  • New visual symptoms need immediate assessment. Painful red eyes and red eyes with contact lenses need urgent eye care.

Frequently asked questions

Is dry eye in pregnancy dangerous?

Many cases can be managed, but it is not safe to call every eye symptom harmless. Severe untreated dry eye can damage the eye surface, and another condition may resemble dryness. Persistent irritation needs an examination; new vision changes, a painful red eye or pain looking at light require urgent assessment.

How long does it last?

Pregnancy-related symptoms often improve after birth, but the timing varies and some changes last into breastfeeding. There is no guaranteed few-week deadline. Seek reassessment for persistent symptoms rather than waiting indefinitely.

What can I do at home?

Take screen breaks, blink fully, reduce direct airflow and smoke, and use glasses if lenses irritate. Ask about a suitable lubricant and gentle closed-lid hygiene if needed. These steps do not replace care for pain, visual changes or continuing symptoms.

Can I use artificial tears while pregnant?

Often a suitable lubricant can be chosen. NHS guidance permits carmellose sodium during pregnancy and breastfeeding, but check the exact product with a pharmacist or eye-care professional. This is not approval for every redness-relief or medicated drop.

Can I keep wearing contact lenses?

Only if they remain comfortable and your eye-care professional considers them suitable. Remove uncomfortable lenses, use glasses and maintain proper hygiene without water exposure. A red eye with contact lenses needs urgent assessment, even without severe pain.

Will extra water, vitamins or fish oil cure it?

No cure is guaranteed. Maintain ordinary hydration and a balanced pregnancy diet, and follow your maternity supplement advice. Do not self-treat with high-dose supplements, vitamin A/retinol or cod-liver oil. Adult omega-3 trial results do not establish a pregnancy dry-eye treatment.

Is rose water or cooled boiled water safe as eye drops?

Do not use homemade liquids as eye drops. Eye medicines need appropriate sterile manufacture and handling; boiling a home mixture does not make it a validated ophthalmic product. External care of closed lids with a clean cloth is a separate measure.

When should I get help immediately?

Contact maternity care immediately for a new visual change during pregnancy or after birth, or for another pre-eclampsia warning symptom such as a severe headache or pain below the ribs. Seek emergency eye care for new sight change or loss, pain looking at light, or a red eye with severe headache and nausea. A painful red eye or red eye with contact lenses needs urgent assessment. Do not wait for every warning sign or drive yourself to emergency care.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
